paras: The lynching of Arthur Stewart was the killing of a Black prisoner in the town calaboose at Pineapple, Wilcox County, Alabama, early on December 26, 1903, by a mob that struck him on the head, poured kerosene over him and set the building on fire. The fire spread through the business district, and although a coroner's jury charged five men with murder, a grand jury found no true bill. Alabama and Black papers alike stressed that Stewart had not done the shooting that prompted the attack.

According to inquest evidence reported by the Birmingham Age-Herald, four white and four Black men were shooting craps near the Pineapple depot on December 22 when Clinton "Pig" Melton quarreled with a Black man, John Westley, whose pistol went off in a scuffle and wounded Melton. Stewart reportedly picked up his gun and walked away, though Melton claimed Stewart had drawn it on him. The constable, Walter Stewart, Melton's brother-in-law, swore out warrants charging Westley with assault to murder and Arthur Stewart with "presenting a gun"; Westley fled. He put Arthur Stewart in the calaboose on Christmas Day; wire reports said Melton's friends "swore vengeance."

At about 4 a.m. on December 26, with the town marshal sick, the calaboose lock was broken, Stewart's skull was cracked by a blow, and his body and the building were soaked with kerosene and fired. The Montgomery Advertiser's correspondent reported that the jail had been fired "to destroy evidence of the crime." A strong wind carried the flames through a seed house, a cotton warehouse, the post office and eight or nine stores, a loss of $35,000 to $50,000.

A coroner's jury was empaneled that day, and about 200 citizens meeting under J. A. Matherson raised a $1,000 reward and asked Solicitor W. W. Quarles to seek a special term of court. The jury returned a sealed verdict on December 29, and Emmet Barlow, Evander Melton, the constable Walter C. Stewart, his brother Pressley Stewart and Robert Ray were arrested and charged with murder.

The preliminary hearing on January 1 collapsed when the presiding justice was disqualified because his property had burned and the remaining justices declined to sit, which the Age-Herald called "a farce comedy." After Governor Jelks said he lacked authority, Circuit Judge John Moore ordered a special term at Camden. The Montgomery Advertiser reported that a first grand jury's true bills were quashed because a juror had served on his brother's summons, and that a second grand jury, rumored split seven to seven, found no true bill on January 13, freeing the five men. No later indictment appears in the coverage; Melton himself died at Pineapple in late January, of a cause not reported.

The wire story ran under headlines such as "To Hide a Lynching" from Kansas to South Dakota, saying only that the mob "is thought to have" fired the jail. Copies spelled the name "Stuart" or "Stowert," some placed the town in Arkansas, and an Indianapolis Journal digest reversed the roles, calling Arthur Stuart the white murder victim.

Alabama papers condemned the mob. The Age-Herald called the lynching "absolutely inexcusable," said the mob "wanted blood," and later called Stewart "an innocent negro" guilty of nothing more than a craps game. A Montgomery Advertiser column quoted a traveler who said the perpetrators "have no supporters," and the Richmond Times-Dispatch and Indianapolis Journal used the case to denounce mobs.

In the Black press, which took up the story a week later, the Cleveland Gazette printed the wire paragraph, while the Chicago Broad Ax mocked "the good Christians of Pineapple" and their "expensive lynching bee." The American Baptist said little attention would have been paid to the lost life had no property burned. The Richmond Planet's "Trouble at Pineapple" insisted Stewart "had committed no crime" and that only a fire which "touched the nerve-centres of the white man's pocket" had brought demands for punishment.

The charge against Stewart varied: "attempted murder" (Montgomery Advertiser), "accomplice" (wire), "accessory" (a traveler), and "presenting a gun" (the more detailed inquest evidence). The wire dated the shooting December 23, the inquest December 22, and only the Indianapolis Journal said Stewart was "burned to death" rather than killed before the fire.

reader.title: Lynching of Arthur Stewart
bases: A mob broke into the Pineapple calaboose and killed a Black prisoner held on a warrant arising from the shooting of a white man, then burned the building (A3, A5, A19).

Stewart was killed in jail by a 'mob' that the wire said acted from vengeance for Melton's shooting, and a coroner's jury charged five men with his murder (A1, A3, A19, A28); the killing had no lawful authority and the papers uniformly called it a lynching (A3, A11).

The Montgomery Advertiser's Pineapple correspondent, the Birmingham Age-Herald's Selma correspondent, the national wire and the inquest evidence all agree that a mob killed Stewart in the calaboose and fired it (A3, A5, A6, A19).

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: One of several Black men shot Melton; a man said to be his accomplice was jailed Christmas Day; Melton's friends 'swore vengeance' and a mob struck him on the head, poured kerosene on him and is 'thought to have' fired the jail.

accounts.label: Montgomery Advertiser local correspondent
accounts.gist: Stewart, jailed for attempted murder, was killed by the mob and the jail set afire to destroy evidence; his charred body was found in the ruins.

accounts.label: Coroner's-jury evidence (Age-Herald)
accounts.gist: Westley's pistol went off in a scuffle and wounded Melton; Stewart picked up his gun and walked away, or by Melton's claim drew it on him, and was charged only with presenting a gun; the mob broke the lock, cracked his skull and burned the building.

accounts.label: Black press editorials
accounts.gist: Stewart had committed no crime, the shooter had escaped, and white indignation arose because of the property burned.

framing.detail: Headlines such as 'To Hide a Lynching' and 'Lynch and Fire Jail' stressed the fire and losses; copy said only that the mob 'is thought to have' fired the jail.
The Birmingham Age-Herald called the lynching 'absolutely inexcusable', said the mob 'wanted blood', and called the victim 'an innocent negro'.
The Montgomery Advertiser quoted a traveler that the perpetrators 'have no supporters' and later recalled 'an innocent negro'.
The Richmond Times-Dispatch ('The Way of the Mob') and Indianapolis Journal used the case to denounce mobs.
The Richmond Planet, Broad Ax and American Baptist mocked white indignation as driven by property loss; the Planet called Stewart innocent.
The Cleveland Gazette ran the wire paragraph without comment.
